nodes.name: PAN nanofiber preparation and carbonization
nodes.procedure: 2 g of polyacrylonitrile (PAN, 150 000 Mw) was dissolved in 13 g of N,N-dimethylformamide (99.8%) with magnetic stirring at room temperature at 300 rpm. After the solution was homogeneously stirred at 80°C for 12 h, electrospinning was conducted. The polymer solution was placed in a syringe with a metal nozzle (23 G), and a voltage of 10 kV was applied between the collector and the metal nozzle. The distance from the needle to the collector was fixed at 20 cm, and the feeding rate was 10 μL/min. After electrospinning, the free-standing PAN NF membrane was gently detached with tweezers. The PAN nanofibers were stabilized in air at 553 K for 1 h and carbonized under argon at 1173 K for 2 h.

nodes.name: Metal precursor solution preparation
nodes.procedure: All precursor solutions were synthesized by mixing MCl_x H_y precursors (0.1 M) with the precursors dissolved in ethanol. Precursors included chloroplatinic(IV) acid hydrate, cobalt(II) chloride, copper(II) chloride, nickel(II) chloride, tin(II) chloride, palladium(II) chloride, ruthenium(III) chloride hydrate, and iron(III) chloride hexahydrate.
nodes.method: Mixing metal chloride precursors in ethanol

nodes.name: Multi-metallic nanoparticle electrode fabrication via carbothermal shock
nodes.procedure: Prepared carbon nanofiber substrates were attached to quartz using silver paste and copper tape. After the substrates were fixed, the metal precursor solution was dropped on the substrate with heating at 80°C. The total solution volume was 200 μL. After the evaporation of ethanol, the carbothermal shock was conducted to fabricate multi-metallic nanoparticles with heating at 300 ms under Ar at 2000 K.

nodes.description: HER performance evaluation of Pt₀.₆₅Ru₀.₃₀Ni₀.₀₅ catalyst via linear sweep voltammetry and electrochemical characterization
nodes.source_text: The Pt₀.₆₅Ru₀.₃₀Ni₀.₀₅ catalyst exhibited an HER overpotential of 54.2 mV, which is superior to that of the pure Pt catalyst. Electrochemical testing was conducted using a three-electrode setup with 0.5 M H₂SO₄ as electrolyte, Ag/AgCl reference electrode, and carbon rod counter electrode. Cyclic voltammetry was conducted at a scan rate of 5 mV/s from 0.05 to -0.8 V versus RHE with IR-correction applied. The Tafel slope of the Pt₀.₆₅Ru₀.₃₀Ni₀.₀₅ catalyst was lower than that of Pt, indicating hydrogen desorption occurred more efficiently. The charge-transfer resistance was considerably less than those of unary metal systems, suggesting rapid electron transfer.

nodes.description: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy of Pt₀.₆₅Ru₀.₃₀Ni₀.₀₅ catalyst for charge-transfer resistance analysis
nodes.source_text: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy was conducted using the same conditions as mentioned above with -0.2 V versus RHE and a scan rate from 10 mHz to 100 kHz. The comparison of the semicircle diameter revealed that the charge-transfer resistance of the Pt₀.₆₅Ru₀.₃₀Ni₀.₀₅ catalyst is considerably less than those of unary metal systems, suggesting rapid electron transfer.

nodes.description: HER performance evaluation of pure Pt catalyst via Tafel analysis
nodes.source_text: Tafel and Nyquist plots were also fitted for unary catalysts and the best performing catalyst to understand the electrochemical behavior and verify its tendency with the active-learning result. The Tafel slope of the Pt₀.₆₅Ru₀.₃₀Ni₀.₀₅ catalyst was lower than that of Pt, which indicated hydrogen desorption over the Pt₀.₆₅Ru₀.₃₀Ni₀.₀₅ catalyst occurred more efficiently than that over the Pt catalyst.

nodes.evidence_snippet: First, the formation of Pt-Ru-Ni alloy nanoparticles was observed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (Figure 4a). These alloy nanoparticles were well dispersed over the substrate, with a uniform size of 9±3.14 nm.

nodes.characterization_summary: TEM-EDS mapping confirms well-mixed Pt, Ru, and Ni in the ternary nanoparticles with average diameter of approximately 9 nm, indicating solid solution formation without significant phase separation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Pt-Ru-Ni alloy formation was investigated by TEM-energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (TEM-EDS) mapping (Figure 4b): These fabricated metal nanoparticles comprised well-mixed Pt, Ru, and Ni, with an average nanoparticle diameter of ≈9 nm, suggesting that the three metals in the ternary nanoparticles are well mixed as a solid solution without significant phase separation.

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS analysis reveals that after carbothermal shock, elements are mainly in metallic state compared to oxidation state before CTS. Atomic composition determined as 73.9-77.8% Pt, 18.6-21.5% Ru, and 3.6-4.6% Ni. Chloride peak almost disappears after fabrication.
nodes.evidence_snippet: To confirm the component and composition of each element in the fabricated nanoparticles, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and TEM-EDS were conducted (Figure 4c). XPS and EDS spectra shown in Figure 4c and Figure S5, Supporting Information, respectively, revealed that considerable amounts of Pt, Ru, and Ni are detected. In addition, after CTS, the elements were mainly found to be in the metallic state compared to the oxidation state before CTS (Figure S7, Supporting Information).

nodes.characterization_summary: Linear sweep voltammetry measurement of hydrogen evolution reaction overpotential at 20 mA/cm² current density shows Pt₀.₆₅Ru₀.₃₀Ni₀.₀₅ catalyst exhibits 54.2 mV overpotential, significantly lower than pure Pt (68.2 mV) and Pt₀.₇Ru₀.₃ (65.6 mV) catalysts.
nodes.evidence_snippet: After catalyst fabrication, electrochemical analysis was conducted to characterize the catalytic performance of the synthesized nanoparticles by measuring overpotential at a current density of 20 mAcm⁻² via linear sweep voltammetry (Figure 1c)... First, the overpotential of the Pt₀.₆₅Ru₀.₃₀Ni₀.₀₅ catalyst was significantly lower than those of the pure Pt catalyst and the Pt₀.₇Ru₀.₃ catalyst synthesized by the same method (i.e., 68.2 and 65.6 mV), respectively (Figure 4d).
